subject: Banking
title: Bernie Madoff's Bank Enablers
description: A micro-lesson that makes Bernie Madoff's Bank Enablers usable.

hook.text: Bernie Madoff ran a $65 billion Ponzi scheme for decades.

buildup.text: Madoff's returns were impossibly consistent: 10-12% every year regardless of market conditions.

discovery.text: JPMorgan filed a suspicious activity report with UK authorities but not with US regulators.

twist.text: JPMorgan paid $2.6 billion for failing to report suspicious activity.

climax.text: Banks are supposed to be the first line of defense against fraud.

punchline.text: $65 billion Ponzi. Banks saw red flags. They chose fees over reporting.

quiz.question: Why didn't JPMorgan report Madoff to US authorities?
options: They suspected fraud but profited from the banking relationship

details.summary: Major banks like JPMorgan Chase processed billions for Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme despite internal warnings and suspicious activity, raising questions about whether they turned a blind eye to fraud for profit.
details.whyItMatters: Banks serve as gatekeepers of the financial system. When they fail to flag obvious fraud, they become complicit in schemes that destroy the savings of thousands of ordinary investors.
takeaways: JPMorgan paid $2.6 billion in penalties for Madoff-related failures
Internal bank emails showed staff questioned Madoff's returns
Banks are legally required to report suspicious activity

faq.question: Did JPMorgan know about Madoff's fraud?
faq.answer: Internal documents showed bank employees raised concerns about Madoff's impossibly consistent returns. JPMorgan settled for $2.6 billion but did not admit knowingly facilitating the fraud.

faq.question: How could banks miss a $65 billion Ponzi scheme?
faq.answer: Some argue they did not miss it but chose to ignore warning signs because Madoff's accounts were profitable. Banks earned fees processing his transactions while filing minimal suspicious activity reports.
